c.tagline: Nature Island capital where rainforest, reef and hot springs meet the sea.

taxi.fareNote: No meters; the government publishes fixed per-route rates (e.g. town trips, airport transfers, tours) that drivers should quote before departure.

emergency.note: Dominica launched a 911 emergency system that runs alongside the traditional 999 police/fire/ambulance line; both connect to dispatch.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Wotten Waven: Ti Kwen Glo Cho, Wotten Waven

avoid.reason: Petty theft happens around the market and bayfront on busy cruise days; avoid poorly lit lanes after dark.

hood_desc: The compact historic core on the waterfront, with French/colonial-era buildings, the Old Market, cathedral, cruise pier and government offices; best for first-timers who want to walk to restaurants, banks and ferries.
A former fishing village just south of downtown that has become Dominica's dive and whale-watching hub, lined with small waterfront guesthouses; suits divers, snorkelers and marine-life enthusiasts.

A lush inland valley village 15-20 minutes above Roseau near Trafalgar Falls and the botanical gardens, with rainforest lodges and cottages; suits nature lovers and hikers wanting quiet and cooler air.
A tiny mountain hamlet famous for volcanic hot-spring spas, a short drive further into the interior; suits couples and wellness travelers seeking sulphur baths and jungle seclusion.
A residential hillside suburb just north/east of downtown Roseau with guesthouses and long-stay apartments; suits budget travelers, volunteers and longer stays who still want quick access to town.
lodging: Anchorage Hotel, Whale Watch & Dive Center

water.note: Water is drawn from mountain rivers and treated, but bottled water is the safer bet for visitors.

transit.pay: Privately-owned minibuses (recognizable by 'H' or 'HA' license plates) run fixed routes from the Roseau bus terminals to villages island-wide; pay the driver or conductor in cash (EC$) on board, fares are set by route/distance. There is no rechargeable card or app-based payment.
transit.hours: Minibuses generally run roughly 6am-7pm on weekdays with reduced/no service on Sundays and holidays; there is no scheduled night service, so taxis are used after dark.
transit.note: Roseau itself is small and very walkable; minibuses are the main way to reach outlying villages, hot springs and trailheads.

air: Canefield Airport (DCF) - small regional/light-aircraft strip 5km north of Roseau
bus: National minibus network from Roseau's West Bridge and Valley Road terminals to villages island-wide
ferry: L'Express des Iles (Roseau to Guadeloupe, Martinique, St. Lucia)

airport.name: Douglas-Charles Airport (DOM)
airport.drive: 75-90 min via the Imperial Road/Castle Bruce route (winding mountain road)

transit.m: Public minibus to Roseau then transfer (infrequent, not really airport-oriented)

tip.r: A 10% service charge is often added at hotels/restaurants; if not, 10% is appreciated but not obligatory. Taxi drivers are not usually tipped beyond rounding up.

food.name: Callaloo Soup
food.desc: Dominica's velvety green soup of dasheen leaves simmered with coconut milk, thyme and often smoked crab or salt meat, served with a dumpling.

places.name: Pearl's Cuisine
places.note: Longtime Creole kitchen famous locally for its smoked-crab callaloo and daily-changing island plates.

places.name: Palisades Restaurant, Fort Young Hotel
places.note: Hotel dining room that keeps a refined callaloo soup on the menu alongside sea views.

places.name: Papillote Wilderness Retreat
places.note: Rainforest garden restaurant long known for callaloo soup made with dasheen from its own grounds.

food.name: Crab Backs
food.desc: Land-crab meat seasoned with garlic, chives and hot pepper, packed back into the shell and baked - Dominica's classic seaside starter.

places.name: Pearl's Cuisine
places.note: Serves crab backs seasonally when the land crabs run; ask what came in that morning.

places.name: The Great Old House
places.note: Heritage-building restaurant doing traditional Creole seafood including stuffed crab backs.

places.name: Fort Young Hotel Waterfront Terrace
places.note: Reliable place to try crab backs with a rum punch looking over the Caribbean.

food.name: Bakes with Saltfish
food.desc: Puffy fried dough pockets split and filled with sauteed saltfish, onion and pepper - the standard Dominican street breakfast.

places.name: Roseau Old Market
places.note: Morning vendors around the cobbled plaza sell hot bakes and saltfish to office workers.

places.name: Roseau Public Market
places.area: Riverfront, north end of Bay Front
places.note: Saturday-morning market stalls fry bakes to order beside the produce sellers.

places.name: Cornerhouse Cafe
places.note: Cafe in Roseau's oldest stone building serving bakes and local breakfasts with coffee.

food.name: Bouyon
food.desc: Hearty one-pot soup of ground provisions, dumplings, pumpkin and salted or smoked meat - Dominica's Saturday comfort food.

places.name: Pearl's Cuisine
places.note: Cooks bouyon and other one-pot Creole staples on a rotating daily lunch menu.

places.name: Roseau Public Market food stalls
places.note: Cook-shops beside the market ladle out bouyon by the bowl on Saturday mornings.

places.name: Lacou Melrose House
places.note: Local-run kitchen turning out traditional Dominican soups and provision plates.

food.name: Titiwi Accra
food.desc: Fritters of titiwi - tiny translucent river fry netted at river mouths - bound in seasoned batter and fried crisp; a true Dominican delicacy.

places.name: Roseau Public Market
places.note: Vendors sell fresh titiwi in season; nearby cook-shops fry them into accra.

places.name: Pearl's Cuisine
places.note: Puts titiwi accra on the menu when the seasonal run comes in.

places.name: Roseau Old Market
places.note: Snack sellers around the plaza fry accra and other Creole street bites.

food.name: Mountain Chicken Heritage Plate
food.desc: Crapaud, the giant frog once Dominica's national dish, is now fully protected - kitchens tell its story while serving the Creole sides it came with.

places.name: Pearl's Cuisine
places.note: Cooks the old-style Creole plates - provisions, gravies, crayfish - that replaced crapaud on menus.

places.name: Papillote Wilderness Retreat
places.note: Owners are deep in Dominica food heritage and will explain the mountain chicken's decline.

places.name: The Great Old House
places.note: Heritage restaurant serving freshwater crayfish, the accepted stand-in for mountain chicken.

food.name: Sea Moss Drink
food.desc: Thick, sweet, chilled drink of seaweed gel blended with condensed milk, nutmeg and vanilla - Dominica's favourite tonic.

places.name: Roseau Old Market
places.note: Bottled sea moss sold cold from coolers by market vendors most mornings.

places.name: Natural Livity Kulcha Shop
places.note: Ital/vegan shop making sea moss and other bush drinks fresh.

places.name: Roseau Public Market
places.note: Juice stalls mix sea moss to order alongside soursop and passionfruit.

food.name: Bush Rum
food.desc: Local white rum steeped with herbs, bark and spice - names like bois bande and lapo kabwit are poured from jars at every rum shop.

places.name: Fort Young Hotel Balas Bar
places.note: Easy, comfortable introduction to Dominican rums and rum punches for visitors.

places.name: Ruins Rock Cafe
places.note: Open-air bar in old stone ruins pouring local rum infusions in a lively setting.

places.name: Roseau Old Market rum shops
places.note: Small neighbourhood bars around the plaza keep jars of spiced bush rum on the counter.

landmarks: Roseau Cathedral (Our Lady of Fair Haven)
This grand Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral, built from volcanic stone in the early 1900s, anchors Roseau's skyline and remains the spiritual heart of Dominica.
Fort Young
This 18th-century British fort overlooking the Caribbean Sea has been transformed into a historic hotel, blending colonial cannon-lined ramparts with sweeping ocean views.
Dominica Botanic Gardens
Sprawling across 40 lush acres since 1890, these gardens showcase exotic tropical flora and a famous school bus crushed by a fallen baobab tree during Hurricane David.
Old Market Square (Roseau Market)
Once a site of slave auctions, this cobblestoned square now bursts with color as vendors sell spices, crafts, and produce beneath the shade of an old saman tree.
Trafalgar Falls
Twin waterfalls nicknamed 'Mother and Father' plunge into a rainforest pool near hot sulfur springs, making this one of the most photographed sights on the Nature Isle.
Champagne Reef
Volcanic vents release streams of warm bubbles through this shallow reef, giving snorkelers the surreal sensation of swimming through champagne.
Boiling Lake
The world's second-largest hot spring, this bubbling, slate-grey cauldron hidden deep in Morne Trois Pitons National Park rewards a grueling hike with an otherworldly sight.
Emerald Pool
A short rainforest trail leads to this glowing green swimming hole fed by a cascading waterfall, framed by ferns and moss-draped boulders.
Titou Gorge
This narrow, dramatic volcanic gorge with cool black-rock walls and a hidden waterfall drew fame as a filming location for Pirates of the Caribbean.
Morne Bruce
Perched high above Roseau, this scenic overlook offers panoramic views of the capital's red rooftops, the Caribbean Sea, and the cruise ships docked below.

train.note: Dominica has no railway of any kind. Getting around means minibuses or the inter-island ferry.

bus.note: No international buses (island). Privately run public minibuses (H-plated) serve towns across Dominica, leaving Roseau from the stands around the Old Market and West Bridge / New Town areas.

ferry.note: The inter-island fast ferry leaves from the Roseau Ferry Terminal on the Bayfront. Guadeloupe and Martinique are the core links (St Lucia less frequent); bring your passport as these are international crossings. Check the timetable, as sailings run only on certain days.
